Industry News: Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health problems can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health problems can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg noted this life-stage breakdown is vital, especially for risk reduction.

She mentioned challenges with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg mentioned.

In a recent development, suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive initiative for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

Industry observers note that “These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are vital windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

Industry observers note that the authors note several age-related warning signs of heart concerns. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” stated Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

It has been revealed that the authors of that report listed several steps they mentioned could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Sources indicate that weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan stated women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • In a recent development, environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

In a recent development, environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a new, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

In a recent development, “It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, stated in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

It has been revealed that the idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

Breaking: Do You Have a Work Spouse? Here's What Research Notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Last week, I found myself running against one of my closest friends for an elected leadership position in a professional organization.
  • When it was my turn to introduce myself, I blurted out that my opponent was my "work spouse" and that I would be absolutely thrilled if they won.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Last week, I found myself running against one of my closest friends for an elected leadership position in a professional organization.

When it was my turn to introduce myself, I blurted out that my opponent was my "work spouse" and that I would be absolutely thrilled if they won. And I meant it (although they may have wished I'd not introduced them in that way).

It has been revealed that the two of us collaborate on research, are currently co-editing a book, and have developed a friendship that extends well beyond our professional responsibilities. We celebrate each other's accomplishments, offer advice, and understand the sometimes ridiculous aspects of academia that can be difficult to explain to anyone outside it.

It has been revealed that just as I was about to post a selfie of us on Instagram with a quick little caption about appreciating my work spouse, I remembered that my dear friend, the late Dr. Chad McBride, had actually published research on this very topic. So, naturally, I decided to blog about it instead.

Sources indicate that you've probably heard someone refer to a colleague as their "work wife" or "work husband." Maybe you've even used the term yourself. But what makes someone a work spouse rather than simply a friend or colleague at work?

In a recent development, in 2015, communication scholars M. Chad McBride and Karla Mason Bergen examined how people characterized their work-spouse relationships. Analyzing responses from 269 participants, they identified recurring characteristics, including trust, honesty, loyalty, respect, emotional connection, and mutual support.

Recent findings suggest that based on these findings, they defined work spouses as close, platonic workplace friends who share a strong emotional connection and provide support for one another. Despite the marital terminology, these relationships are generally understood as nonromantic and nonsexual.

I've always found the term particularly interesting because my parents are both actual spouses and work spouses. They're professors in the same discipline, and I grew up watching them navigate their personal and professional lives together. So when I call my friend my work spouse, I'm describing something quite different from the relationship I've watched my parents share. Still, both relationships involve professional collaboration, mutual support, and an understanding of each other's work.

It has been revealed that think about how much of our lives we spend working. We navigate stressful deadlines, celebrate accomplishments, complain about frustrating policies, and occasionally wonder why we chose our particular professions in the first place. Naturally, we develop relationships with the people experiencing those things alongside us.

And sometimes, those relationships become particularly meaningful because our co-workers understand things about our professional lives that people outside our workplaces might not.

For instance, my work spouse understands why I might be nervous to present a fresh idea, excited by a revise and resubmit, or frustrated about a particular obligation. I don't have to spend time explaining the context before getting to the actual story, and sometimes that can be really nice.

But it's more than having someone who understands your workplace. Sometimes, that person is also helping you get the work done.

The two of us work on projects together, but we also spend time working independently alongside one another. We bounce ideas off each other, provide feedback, and hold each other accountable for making progress. I find that I'm often more productive when we're working together, even when we're tackling entirely different tasks.

It has been revealed that these experiences are reflected in McBride and Bergen's findings. Participants described work spouses as people they could confide in, seek advice from, and rely on during stressful periods. Others talked about having someone who motivated them, challenged them professionally, or simply made difficult workdays more enjoyable.

According to recent reports, and I imagine these experiences aren't unique to academia. Think about teachers planning lessons together, nurses navigating difficult shifts, or colleagues working toward a shared deadline.

What I find interesting is that these friendships aren't just about having someone to vent to. They can also shape how we experience the work itself.

Of course, mixing friendship and work isn't always straightforward. Management scholars Whitman and Mandeville (2021) explored how work-spouse relationships blur the boundaries between our professional and personal lives, including potential complications involving favoritism, romantic partners, and competing responsibilities.

But I think sometimes, the challenges are simply those that come with being close friends who also work together.

My work spouse and I have certainly had our rough patches. We've had to figure out how to support each other as friends while also being honest and productive collaborators. We've had plenty of conversations about what we need from one another, including when one of us needs encouragement and when one of us needs to be told we're being unreasonable and need to chill out.

Industry observers note that this is something McBride and his colleagues explored further. In two subsequent studies, McBride, Allison Thorson, and Bergen (2020a, 2020b) examined how work spouses manage privacy and navigate one another's feelings and professional identities. Their research illustrates that even close workplace friendships involve decisions about what to share, when to speak up, and how to support one another.

And, for what it's worth, I don't think every close workplace friendship needs a special label. But I do think these relationships deserve the same attention and care we give to our friendships outside of work.

According to recent reports, mcBride, M. C., & Bergen, K. M. (2015). Work spouses: Defining and understanding a “newly introduced” relationship. Communication Studies, 66(5), 487–508. https://doi.org/10.1080/10510974.2015.1029640.

Sources indicate that mcBride, M. C., Thorson, A. R., & Bergen, K. M. (2020a). An examination of individually performed and (co)managed facework: Unique communication within the work-spouse relationship. Communication Studies, 71(4), 489–510. https://doi.org/10.1080/10510974.2020.1749866.

McBride, M. C., Thorson, A. R., & Bergen, K. M. (2020b). Privacy rule decision criteria: An examination of core and catalyst criteria that shape disclosures in the work-spouse relationship. Management Communication Quarterly, 34(4), 527–557. https://doi.org/10.1177/0893318920949328.

In a recent development, whitman, M. V., & Mandeville, A. (2021). Blurring the lines: Exploring the work spouse phenomenon. Journal of Management Inquiry, 30(3), 285–299. https://doi.org/10.1177/1056492619882095.

The world’s biggest oil shock could give EVs and solar a boost

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home.
  • Recent findings suggest that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran.
  • “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home. That’s one of the massive takeaways from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) new “World Energy Outlook 2026,” which examines how the biggest oil supply shock on record could speed up the shift to EVs and solar.

Recent findings suggest that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran. Well-stocked oil inventories helped buffer the initial shock, and the IEA coordinated a release of emergency oil reserves. Some Gulf oil took routes around the strait. Atlantic Basin exporters shipped more, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now more of the burden is falling on consumers, who are paying higher prices and cutting back.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

According to recent reports, the IEA has seen EV sales jump in some countries hit by the crisis, along with increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For countries that import a lot of oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can help reduce their exposure to the next fuel price spike.

Industry observers note that “The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” stated energy think tank Ember’s chief analyst Dave Jones. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think. So much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 comes from the desire to have cheaper and more secure energy.”.

Sources indicate that solar leads renewables growth in every scenario the IEA models, and nuclear power is growing strongly, too. Energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push to use more homegrown energy could have a very different effect in parts of Asia, where some countries that import oil and gas have plenty of their own coal and could keep burning it for longer.

Industry observers note that the world was already using a lot more electricity before the crisis. Since 2019, electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand, outpacing global economic growth. Everything from industrial motors and air conditioners to EVs, heat pumps, and data centers is driving that growth. Electricity comes close to 30% of the energy the world actually uses by 2035 in each of the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.

Before the crisis, around 20 million barrels of oil a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping stays risky, new pipelines could route some of those barrels around the strait, while buyers turn to other suppliers or use less oil. In that case, the IEA notes the amount of oil that needs to pass through Hormuz could drop to 8.5 million barrels a day in 2030 and below 2 million by 2035. The Middle East would still be the world’s largest oil-exporting region.

Recent findings suggest that if the conflict is resolved, oil and gas supply could bounce back. A delayed wave of liquefied natural gas could also help bring prices down even as buyers refill their inventories. Faster electrification could take some of the demand out of both markets.

The world is now using more energy to cool its buildings than to heat them for the first time, the IEA says. By 2035, the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third. Energy needs rise gradually in advanced economies, growth slows in China, and India and Southeast Asia lead faster increases across other emerging and developing economies.

Then there’s AI. Under the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already running into grid and supply chain constraints, and in some places, local opposition. The IEA also flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

Energy-related CO2 emissions stay around today’s levels under current policies. They start to fall under stated policies and drop further in the IEA’s Additional Response Case, which looks at what could happen if governments respond more strongly to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require. The current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, and the latest round of national climate pledges indicates little sign that countries are speeding up energy-sector emissions cuts.

According to recent reports, the green agenda always come in a second place because people cannot see that far out in the future. Stability of the economy and energy independence are much more notable drivers and have immediate impact. Local environment boosts like clean air in cities are also immediate drivers while long term reduced medical bills are not. The oil industry is challenged becuase, unlike previous numerous crises, there is an alternative and the green is the newly introduced black.

There’s a more immediate cost, too. More people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, but higher fuel prices and shortages threaten to slow that progress. Around 720 million people still live without electricity, and nearly 2 billion cook with polluting fuels or technologies.

How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym.
  • As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.
  • Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

Recent findings suggest that “It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”.

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

In a recent development, “These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” indicates Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, states Carr.

Recent findings suggest that “They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly crucial, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

Industry observers note that “They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” notes Carr.

In a recent development, picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”.

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” claims Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”.

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” indicates Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”.

Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

Recent findings suggest that this is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently debuted Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

Industry observers note that the Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Industry observers note that instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

It has been revealed that as for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for newly introduced players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

Cuckoo sizes it for eight cups of uncooked rice, enough to yield about 16 cups cooked, so it suits a household that goes through rice most nights or anyone who batch cooks for the week. The organization’s fuzzy logic system adjusts heat and timing as the pot cooks, and the nonstick inner pot and auto clean mode keep cleanup short.

Induction heat without the pressure-cooker price.

Induction is the major step up from a basic heating plate. Cuckoo says the system in the Cuckoo 8-Cup Induction Heating Rice Cooker heats the whole inner pot instead of only the bottom, and at $191.98 (40% off) it costs far less than the brand’s pressure models. It has 12 menu modes, including GABA rice, scorched rice, porridge and yogurt. Cuckoo also lists a turbo mode that cooks a single serving in about 20 minutes, plus voice guidance in English, Korean and Chinese.

Pressure when you want it, open cooking when you don’t.

Twin pressure is the feature to know here. The Cuckoo 6-Cup Twin Pressure Rice Cooker lets you pick pressure cooking for stickier, chewier rice or non-pressure cooking for fluffier grains, and Cuckoo gives it 16 menu options to cover both. It holds six cups uncooked (12 cooked) and talks you through settings in three languages. It’s $232.55 during the sale, or 32% off.

Seven temperature presets for tea drinkers.

The deepest discount in the sale isn’t a rice cooker. The Cuckoo 1.7L Electric Glass Kettle with Tea Infuser drops to $47.90, which is 47% off. Cuckoo builds it with seven temperature presets from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, a detachable infuser for loose-leaf tea and a keep-warm function that the company notes runs up to two hours after boiling. The 1,500-watt base heats a full 1.7 liters.

Industry News: Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported.
  • Recent findings suggest that charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to fresh research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Recent findings suggest that charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, stated Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that “By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz stated the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

According to recent reports, she said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he noted. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

According to recent reports, A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

Industry observers note that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy noted.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

Sources indicate that by age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy noted. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

According to recent reports, wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, debuted in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham noted the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

Industry observers note that the study indicated links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also stated the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

In a recent development, cunningham noted adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

Porsche’s newest electric car is a tiny 50 mph replica of a legendary racer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a upcoming Taycan or Macan EV.
  • Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.
  • Sources indicate that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the company before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a upcoming Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.

Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.

Sources indicate that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the company before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its stunning Bentley Blower recreation.

Now the company has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.

There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.

The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.

It has been revealed that despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the upcoming electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.

The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).

It has been revealed that for those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.

Sources indicate that the attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.

Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.

The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.

Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.

Of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap. Prices start at £69,500 (approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.

It has been revealed that that’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.

And if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

Latest Update: Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.
  • Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.
  • “Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of latest technologies.”.

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

It has been revealed that the campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”.

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

It has been revealed that “Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is key for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski noted. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”.

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

Sources indicate that “A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he remarked. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”.

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”.

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious glitch,” he stated.

While it was a challenging experience, he noted it was also fulfilling.

It has been revealed that “I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he noted. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”.

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he noted.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

It has been revealed that getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

According to recent reports, “We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar remarked. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”.

Sources indicate that as he embraces his 50s, he noted he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

It has been revealed that he also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

Sources indicate that “[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he noted.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

It has been revealed that “I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar remarked.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”.

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he stated.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”.

#143971. Industry News: How to Get What You Really Want

Industry News: How to Get What You Really Want

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • I've played tennis all my life, first in school and now recreationally in adult leagues.
  • Years ago, I heard a line in a commercial: "If only I didn't have to work, I could have been a pro!".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

I've played tennis all my life, first in school and now recreationally in adult leagues. I've had my wins and losses. Recently, I looked up my computer records—my cumulative record over the last 20 years. A 0.500 win-loss percentage! Couldn't be more perfect.

Years ago, I heard a line in a commercial: "If only I didn't have to work, I could have been a pro!".

I laughed out loud. The irony, of course, is that you have to work precisely because you're not good enough to be a pro!

According to recent reports, even though I rationally knew that my weekend matches didn't matter all that much, when I was younger, I wanted to win so badly! I would have given anything if somebody had told me the secret to winning.

What I didn't understand in my youth, being goal-driven and perhaps a bit intense, was that while commitment and engagement are critical to achieving our goals, obsessive attachment to a particular outcome can sometimes be counterproductive, preventing us from getting closer to what we want so badly.

Sources indicate that one of the brain's remarkable strengths is its ability to focus, learn, and adapt. Sustained attention and practice allow us to develop specialized skills, whether playing the guitar, shooting a basketball, or designing a bridge.

I wrote in a previous post that we become what we attend to. But focus has an opportunity cost. The more intensely we attend to one thing, the less we notice everything else.

I now realize that what my younger self really wanted was to become a better tennis player. Winning had become a proxy for that larger goal. Over time, however, I began to mistake the proxy for the goal itself.

Sources indicate that this isn't advice to say that winning doesn't matter and we should just chill out. It's perfectly fine to want to win and be fiercely competitive on the court. But once I realized that I had become overly attached to winning as proof that I was a good tennis player, I was able to loosen my grip on the outcome.

Recent findings suggest that sure, I still don't like to lose. But by reflecting on what I love about the game—learning and expressing different skills through my body and enjoying time with like-minded players—I've become better able to learn from my losses and mistakes, and to be genuinely in awe of my opponents' amazing plays.

According to recent reports, dancing on the dance floor and losing yourself in the moment can be exhilarating. But sometimes, stepping onto the balcony allows you to reflect and see the larger picture.

It has been revealed that of course, reflecting is easier noted than done, especially when something genuinely matters to us. Not getting a promotion genuinely hurts. It's also OK to leave the dance floor for a while and get a change of scenery. Going on vacation, spending time with family, or removing ourselves from the situation may create some space.

And when we come back, we may have renewed interest in getting that promotion next time around. We can recommit ourselves to work and perhaps make an effort to seek feedback from our colleagues. Or we may realize that we've been sacrificing so much for work and that the promotion was a proxy for the recognition we craved. We may then decide to change course by setting upcoming boundaries or pivoting to a different line of work.

Sources indicate that letting go does not mean that we stop caring or trying. It means loosening our attachment to a particular outcome. We can still want something deeply without letting that desire define us.

And when we let it go a bit, curious things may happen. We may relax, become more open to other possibilities, or feel more comfortable in our own skin. Sometimes, this even helps us achieve what we originally wanted. But that isn't the point—or a guarantee.

Industry observers note that the word "freedom" keeps circling back in my mind here: the ability to choose and re-commit to a goal worth pursuing. This freedom does not necessarily weaken our commitment, but it makes our commitment more meaningful.

Industry observers note that of course, if someone had told my younger self to stop caring so much about winning, I probably wouldn't have listened. I might even have been annoyed. Sometimes, we have to learn these things through our own disappointments.

Recent findings suggest that would my younger self have considered a 0.500 winning record after 20 years a success? Hard to say. But along the way, I made many friends, experienced the ups and downs of competition, and learned not only new skills but also something about myself.

The numbers may not show it, but I would consider that a success.

Sometimes, years later, you get what you once wanted so badly.

Sometimes, you realize that what you want has changed.

Tech Report: Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done.
  • This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.
  • Sources indicate that the updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

Sources indicate that the updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing fresh Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

Bear cub takes award-winning leap of faith

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that for this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award.
  • “Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In bear life, as in human life, sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. A brown bear (Ursus arctos) cub hanging around Anan Creek in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska learned that this summer. Its mom, Gemini, was crossing the creek, and one cub jumped right in. But this cub? Not so sure. It stood waiting at the water’s edge, before jumping in.

Recent findings suggest that for this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award. For those keeping score at home, Gemini won this year’s helicopter mom award.

“Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots for wildlife is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears like Gemini and her cubs. Similar to their chubby counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to gorge on salmon ahead of the long winter, and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear around Anan Creek has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behaviors.
